item.title: Can AI Write Good English Teaching Materials? Only If It Learns From Experts
item.dc:creator: Modern English Australia

item.title: The Expertise Paradox: Why Good ESL Resources Are Getting Harder to Find
item.dc:creator: Modern English Australia
item.description: Millions of free ESL quizzes and worksheets, but how many are any good? A former IELTS examiner on why expertise has become invisible online.
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever previewed 15 Kahoots before finding one you would trust in class? Have you found one that looked perfect, with a good topic, bright images and the right level, only to reach a question halfway through where the “correct” answer was wrong? Play it, and you teach your students a mistake in front of the whole class.

When I was teaching, this happened more often than I would like to admit, and most English teachers I know have a similar story. It points to a problem that the EdTech industry rarely talks about. Finding teaching materials is no longer difficult. Finding good teaching materials is.

The internet solved the content problem

Twenty years ago, the challenge was supply. Today it is the opposite. By 2018, Kahoot alone reported a library of 51 million public kahoots. Add Wordwall, Quizizz, Teachers Pay Teachers, Pinterest and AI generators, and the supply is effectively endless.

The people creating this material are a global community. English now has around 1.53 billion speakers, and roughly 390 million of them speak it as a first language (Ethnologue, 2025). That means about three in four English speakers learned it as an additional language. This is one of the great success stories of modern communication.

It also means that the people writing English quizzes come from every educational system, every language background, and every level of training, from postgraduate linguists to someone who made a quiz on their lunch break.

What the research says about shared teaching resources

This is not just a feeling. When researchers have looked at popular teacher-shared materials, the results are sobering.

A 2019 Fordham Institute study asked expert reviewers to rate more than 300 of the most downloaded English lessons on three major sharing sites. Most materials were attractive and largely free of obvious errors. However, 64% were rated as either not to be used or probably not worth using. The accompanying assessments were especially weak.

A 2023 study of best-selling history resources on Teachers Pay Teachers found something similar: well designed visually, but 70% of moderate or low quality, and 30% potentially harmful to students.

The most telling detail is that the most downloaded resources were not the best ones. Popularity and quality had separated.

The internet rewards visibility. Teaching rewards knowledge, experience and judgement. These are not the same thing.

The Expertise Paradox

This leads to what I call the Expertise Paradox of EdTech.

The teachers best able to create excellent resources are often the ones who need online resources least. Experienced teachers draw on years of practice, formal training and linguistic knowledge. They can spot a weak distractor at a glance, adapt an activity for their group, or write something better themselves. They are also busy teaching, marking and mentoring, so they publish less.

Less experienced teachers rely more on shared materials, and they often have more reason to share, adapt and publish online. The result is a feedback loop:

  1. New teachers rely on existing internet resources.
  2. New resources are adapted from those same resources.
  3. Errors and weak task design get copied, not corrected.
  4. AI systems are trained on the same repositories.

Over time, internet consensus begins to compete with genuine expertise.

This is not about native speakers

It would be easy to misread this argument, so I want to be clear. The problem is not nationality, and it is not whether the creator is a native speaker.

Research in English language teaching has long criticised native-speakerism, the assumption that native-speaker teachers are automatically better. Non-native English-speaking teachers make up at least 80% of English language educators worldwide. Many of the best teachers I have worked with learned English as an additional language.

When I was checking quizzes for my own classes, the errors fell into two groups. Some were plain carelessness: a native speaker who had not proofread, distractors that did not work, or questions with two possible answers. Others were patterns any experienced English teacher recognises: missing or incorrect articles, awkward collocations, and structures carried over from another language. These are the exact errors we spend our careers helping students overcome. (I collected a few favourites in Kahoot!, Baamboozle and Wordwall’s Funny English.)

The real issue is that expertise has become invisible. To a platform, a carefully built activity by a TESOL-qualified teacher and a rushed quiz by an untrained tutor are simply two quizzes. To the teacher using them, they are not remotely equivalent.

How to check a quiz in 60 seconds

Until platforms make expertise visible, the filtering falls to us. Before using any shared activity, check:

  • The answer key. Read every “correct” answer, not just the questions.
  • The distractors. Wrong options should be plausibly wrong, never accidentally right.
  • Articles and collocations. These are where errors hide most often.
  • The level. Make sure the vocabulary and grammar match your learners.
  • The creator. Look for a profile, a qualification, or a body of consistent work.

Expertise should be visible again

The internet has dramatically increased the supply of educational content. It has not increased the visibility of expertise. That is the gap Modern English is built to close: teaching tools and resources designed by qualified, experienced English teachers, so you spend your time teaching rather than checking someone else’s answer key.

item.title: What Are English Tests Actually Testing?
item.dc:creator: Modern English Australia
item.description: Notes from two Duolingo English Test seminars in Sydney: in 2024 the pitch was equity, in 2025 it was cheating rings. Are English tests built to measure English, or to outsmart cheats?
item.content:encoded:
Over the past few years I’ve been going to every tech and exam seminar passing through Sydney, from Pearson’s PTE Academic to the Duolingo English Test (DET) to CELPIP, one of three tests Australia added to its visa list in August 2025.

What strikes me most about high-stakes immigration exams, and their marriage to technology, is that no one is focussed on the purpose or the accuracy of the test. The companies pitching exams to the Australian immigration department are focussed on security.

I’m going to be drawing on anecdotes from the Duolingo English Test seminars in 2024 and 2025, but I think they point to a general pattern in the exam industry. (As of August 2025, the Duolingo test was not on the list of nine tests Australia accepts for visas, so it is very much still pitching. The accepted tests are IELTS Academic and IELTS General Training, Pearson’s PTE Academic, Cambridge English, TOEFL iBT, OET, LanguageCert Academic, CELPIP General and the Michigan English Test.)

In 2024 Duolingo spoke of ‘equity’: a test which someone in rural India could take at home, on a device as simple as their phone, rather than take the exhausting train ride into crazy old Mumbai. The selling point was that the test was cheaper and more convenient. It takes about an hour and costs around US$70, with no appointment and no test centre.

It has a few innovations in pedagogy that I think need more testing. For instance, the test is adaptive. You’ll be asked some questions early in the test, and your performance then dictates how hard the rest of the test is. If you get the easier questions there is a low ceiling, as these tests are judged on sophistication, not just accuracy.

In 2025 the winds had turned. The free masterclass run by Duolingo and English Australia, ‘Integrity, Authenticity & the Future of Assessment’, held at the Sheraton Grand Sydney Hyde Park on 25 September, was a truly fascinating seminar with little to do with what the test tested and whether it was accurate or useful. Instead, Basim Baig, Duolingo’s Head of Security, facilitated a really interesting session on cheating rings, going into a world which I had glimpses of as an examiner in India: highly organised, technical and determined cheating gangs. The other speakers were Professor Phillip Dawson of Deakin University and Duolingo Assessment Specialist Dr Masha Kostromitina, and one advertised highlight was ‘the economics of cheating — and how to disrupt it’.

The Duolingo test, which was cheap and at home, now requires a second camera on a phone or tablet as well as the computer’s webcam, and a scan of your room instructed by an AI. Duolingo also hires thousands of moderators, not to check the test scores but to watch back video for signs of cheating rings.

For instance, one set of photographs showed the same room with different curtains. The room had been set up to cheat the AI scanner, and the ring thought they could change the curtains and fool the moderators.

My question for you is: what is the purpose of these tests? To outsmart cheaters, or to actually test English that is fit for purpose? Tell me on the contact page.

References

[1] Duolingo and English Australia. Masterclass invitation, ‘Integrity, Authenticity & the Future of Assessment’, Sheraton Grand Sydney Hyde Park, 25 September 2025.

[2] Duolingo English Test. Secondary camera requirement, 28 October 2024. https://blog.englishtest.duolingo.com/duolingo-english-test-secondary-camera

[3] Coursera. What Is the Duolingo English Test? https://www.coursera.org/articles/duolingo-english-test

[4] The PIE News. Australia expands accepted English language tests for visa applications, August 2025. https://thepienews.com/australia-expands-accepted-english-language-tests-for-visa-applications/

item.title: Incidental Learning in the Age of AI
item.dc:creator: Modern English Australia
item.description: Notes from the English Australia and Pearson AI workshop in Sydney: why soft skills matter more than ever, whether teachers should police AI, and the case for incidental learning.
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday I attended English Australia’s Pearson AI workshop, which unofficially happens every year.

Mike Mayor (LinkedIn) came from the UK to Sydney again this year to continue the conversation with Sydney teachers and academic leaders, and to present his data on the international ELICOS industry.

Not the AI apocalypse

Last year the AI workshop was much bigger, which shows how far the ELICOS industry in Australia is shrinking thanks to the cut in student visas.

In 2025 the idea of AI tutors was everywhere, and I expected a doom workshop on how to survive the AI tutor apocalypse. Instead, I was pleasantly surprised. Mayor presented evidence that as AI takes up the slack on the details — the academic assessment and skills students can easily pick up to be future ready — it is the soft skills that computers can’t teach: collaboration, communication, critical thinking, leadership and self-management. And according to his research, that means teachers are needed more than ever.

The Pearson GSE Soft Skills page has more information on the soft skills the Global Scale of English is talking about.

Should teachers police AI?

The workshop began in the same vein, but soon moved on to how to assess students who use AI, and how realistic it is to ban AI for adult students who will find ways around any measures.

Most of the teachers agreed that they should not police AI strictly. That’s not why they became teachers, and the students who really want to learn will monitor their own use.

The main problem, it was suggested, is this: how do you give feedback, and how do you know a student is learning, if they use AI?

AI for the research, students for the thinking?

One suggestion was that students could use AI to source the research and then, with the research at hand, do the critical thinking themselves.

Mayor suggested that the days of students going to libraries and reading through multiple books and chapters to find their information are gone. Now they can use AI to find the evidence and research they want to include in their assignment. And this is efficiency.

But I questioned this. If everybody is using AI to find specific research or sources, they may already have assumptions and biases. They are looking for information that reinforces their bias.

Moreover, if a student spends a lot of time reading, rather than relying on AI to summarise, they get a fuller understanding — and it may occur to them to focus on a new aspect of the topic.

Waiting for the apple to fall

And more, moreover: driving home from the library, stuck in traffic, thinking about dinner, an apple might fall on their head.

I remember the story of the young physics graduate who couldn’t get a university job and was working as a patent clerk. Riding a tram away from the clock tower in Bern, he suddenly had an idea about time. That was Albert Einstein, and the idea became his theory of relativity.

Mayor summed this up as incidental learning.

The group of academic teachers and leaders never managed to come up with a plan, but perhaps apples will fall on their heads about how they can use AI to create future-ready students.

So, what is your experience of incidental learning? Tell me on the contact page.

item.title: Kahoot!, Baamboozle and Wordwall's Funny English
item.dc:creator: Modern English Australia
item.description: Kahoot!, Baamboozle and Wordwall are excellent platforms. The problem is that most of their activities are made by users — and a lot of them contain English mistakes that get taught to students as correct.
item.content:encoded:
There is a strange phenomenon that happens when you teach English long enough.

You open a perfectly innocent-looking classroom game.

You click through the questions.

Everything looks great.

Then suddenly you see it:

"She is having a headache."

Or:

"I am agree."

And you sit there thinking, 'Who made this?'

Welcome to the wonderful world of online teaching games.

The problem isn't the games

Let's get one thing straight: platforms such as Kahoot!, Baamboozle and Wordwall are fantastic teaching tools.

They are quick, engaging and incredibly useful for teachers. They have transformed the way many classrooms approach revision, vocabulary and grammar.

And they work. A 2026 study in GLENS: Global English Insights Journal put Wordwall and Baamboozle head to head with 86 vocational students in Gresik, Indonesia, across six sessions of job-related vocabulary. Both groups improved significantly (p < .001): Wordwall from 61.25 to 76.48, Baamboozle from 60.87 to 80.36.[1]

So the format does its job. It's what gets typed into it that doesn't.

But a very large amount of the material available on these platforms is created by users, and the majority of people teaching English these days aren't native speakers, or aren't very good at English.

In fact, a data search dug up some statistics for me showing that a large proportion of the teachers generating some of these games are from Brazil and Ukraine.

And Kahoot! — which, incidentally, grew out of a research project at a Norwegian university — acknowledges the problem itself. In response to a teacher complaining about grammar mistakes in ready-made Kahoot! activities, the company explained that because so much content is user-generated, it has little control over it.

The other problem is how awkward and clunky they are to make, and I know, because I've done it myself: got so sick of typing into little windows that I skipped the final check and had an embarrassing typo in front of my class.

In other words, the person who created the quiz may have been an excellent teacher.

Meanwhile, Wordwall is a UK-based company, which put out its first digital English games circa 2006 (what other software are you still using from that era?).

Wordwall supports dozens of languages and has an enormous library of teacher-created resources. Its platform currently contains over 118 million activities created by users.

That means you can find absolutely brilliant material. And absolute shitte.

The little mistakes that get passed on

Sometimes it's the little things like:

"I did a mistake."

instead of:

"I made a mistake."

And the non-native teachers making these mistakes, sometimes because they were taught wrong or they are doing a direct translation from their language, might not recognise them when they see it in a game. They may assume the mistake must be correct, and it reinforces their 'funny' English and that of all their students to come.

Missing articles and phrasal verbs

It's probably a bigger issue with missing articles or phrasal verbs, the kind of thing that might change English for the worse. What seems like a waste of time to get right, for students who don't have these in their language, is actually the core of English. An article — "it is on a desk" vs "it is on the desk" — makes English precise. "Get up", "stand up" makes it colourful.

At least the careless native usually notices the mistake, and feels embarrassed in front of the class when they have to admit to it.

Reference

[1] Umayah, E., & Maruf, N. (2026). A Comparative Study of Two Game-Based Digital Platforms on Students' Vocabulary Mastery in EFL Classrooms. GLENS: Global English Insights Journal, 3(2), 188–203. https://doi.org/10.66314/glens.v3i2.672
